faq.a: Direct measurement uses para-aminohippurate clearance; indirect estimates use GFR and the 1.2 factor.
Many drugs are cleared by the kidneys; low RPF reduces clearance, increasing toxicity risk.
faq.q: Why is RPF important for drug dosing?

faq.a: Volume expansion and vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin) can raise RPF in hypovolemia or renal artery stenosis.

exam: What is the relationship between RPF and GFR? — RPF > GFR; GFR is the filtered fraction of RPF.
In a patient with oliguria and high BUN/Cr ratio, what is the most likely cause? — Prerenal azotemia due to low RPF.
How would you interpret a low RPF in a patient with diabetes and normal creatinine? — Early hyperfiltration; monitor for CKD.
Why is para‑aminohippurate clearance preferred over creatinine clearance for RPF? — It is cleared by tubular secretion, not filtration, giving true plasma flow.
What is the effect of renal artery stenosis on RPF? — RPF falls, leading to prerenal AKI and secondary hyperaldosteronism.
In malaria‑associated AKI, which factor most reduces RPF? — Sepsis‑induced vasodilation and hemolysis.
Why might a patient with heart failure have a low RPF? — Elevated central venous pressure causes renal venous congestion and reduced arterial inflow.
ai.title: Renal Plasma Flow
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Renal plasma flow (RPF) is the volume of blood delivered to the kidneys per minute, reflecting renal perfusion and filtration capacity. It is key for interpreting GFR, drug dosing, and renal disease severity.

b: RPF > GFR because some plasma is reabsorbed in the tubules
sections.p: RPF is the amount of plasma that reaches the kidneys each minute. It is usually about 600 mL/min in a healthy adult and is a prerequisite for glomerular filtration.

t.b: Fractional excretion of sodium – tells whether kidneys are conserving or excreting sodium; high FENa suggests intrinsic renal failure.
Measures GFR indirectly; useful when creatinine is unreliable.

b: RPF = Cardiac output × (renal vascular resistance / total systemic resistance)
sections.p: RPF is determined by cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and renal vascular resistance. It is reduced in hypovolemia, sepsis, and renal artery stenosis.

t.b: Assesses renal artery flow; high resistive index indicates renal parenchymal disease.
Detects venous congestion in heart failure, affecting RPF.

b: Low RPF → decreased GFR, oliguria, azotemia
High RPF in hyperfiltration (diabetes) can precede CKD
sections.p: Changes in RPF affect drug clearance, electrolyte balance, and blood pressure regulation. It is crucial in managing acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD).

t.b: Oliguria (<400 mL/24 h) suggests low RPF or tubular failure.
Rises when GFR falls; not a direct measure of RPF but correlated.

b: In malaria‑associated AKI, RPF falls due to hemolysis and sepsis
sections.p: Examiners often ask how RPF is calculated, its clinical significance, and how it changes in common African conditions.

t.b: Low (<20 mEq/L) in prerenal AKI; high (>40) in intrinsic.

b: Low RPF can be intrinsic (e.g., acute tubular necrosis)
sections.p: Students often confuse RPF with GFR, forget that RPF is plasma not whole blood, and misinterpret low RPF as always prerenal.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe oliguria (<200 mL/day), anuria, rising creatinine >1.5 mg/dL within 48 h, hypotension with signs of end‑organ hypoperfusion
